content: Staphylococcus aureus is a common cause of pulmonary infections in young children with cystic fibrosis. To prevent such infections and subsequent lung damage, prophylactic antibiotics are often prescribed. However, the use of antibiotics is associated with potential adverse effects, and prolonged use may increase the risk of colonization or infection with Pseudomonas aeruginosa. This review is an update of a previously published analysis. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effects of continuous oral antibiotic prophylaxis in preventing the acquisition of Staphylococcus aureus in individuals with cystic fibrosis, compared to no prophylaxis. The hypotheses tested included whether prophylaxis improves clinical outcomes such as lung function, survival, and overall health; reduces the presence of Staphylococcus aureus; causes adverse effects such as diarrhea, skin rash, or candidiasis; reduces the presence of other respiratory pathogens; or contributes to antibiotic resistance and colonization with Pseudomonas aeruginosa. The review involved a comprehensive search of databases, journals, conference abstracts, and online trial registries. The most recent searches were conducted in February 2020 for the Cochrane Cystic Fibrosis and Genetic Disorders Group Trials Register and in September 2020 for online trial registries. Randomized controlled trials comparing continuous prophylactic antibiotics (administered for at least one year) to intermittent antibiotics given as needed were included. Participants of any disease severity with cystic fibrosis were eligible. Four studies were included in the review, involving a total of 401 participants aged between zero and seven years at enrollment. One additional study is ongoing. The two older studies had a higher risk of bias, particularly due to lack of blinding and incomplete outcome data, while the two more recent studies were of higher methodological quality. However, even the most recent study had some uncertainty regarding the impact of per-protocol analysis on its results. The overall quality of evidence for all outcomes was judged to be low, primarily due to study design limitations, imprecision, and inconsistency. The findings suggested that prophylactic anti-staphylococcal antibiotics likely have little to no effect on lung function, as measured by FEV1% predicted, after six years of treatment (mean difference: -2.30; 95% confidence interval: -13.59 to 8.99; one study; 119 participants; low-quality evidence). However, prophylaxis may reduce the number of children with one or more isolates of Staphylococcus aureus at two years (odds ratio: 0.21; 95% confidence interval: 0.13 to 0.35; three studies; 315 participants; low-quality evidence). At the two-year mark, there appeared to be little or no effect on nutritional status, as measured by weight z-scores (mean difference: 0.06; 95% confidence interval: -0.33 to 0.45; two studies; 140 participants; low-quality evidence), the need for additional antibiotic courses (odds ratio: 0.18; 95% confidence interval: 0.01 to 3.60; one study; 119 participants; low-quality evidence), or the occurrence of adverse effects (low-quality evidence). There was no significant difference in the number of Pseudomonas aeruginosa isolates between groups at two years (odds ratio: 0.74; 95% confidence interval: 0.45 to 1.23; three studies; 312 participants; low-quality evidence). However, there was a trend suggesting a lower cumulative isolation rate of Pseudomonas aeruginosa in the prophylaxis group at two and three years, which reversed to a higher rate from four to six years. Since the studies reviewed lasted no longer than six years, the long-term effects of prophylactic antibiotics remain unclear. The authors concluded that early initiation of anti-staphylococcal antibiotic prophylaxis in infancy and continuation up to six years of age may reduce the number of children with isolates of Staphylococcus aureus. However, the clinical significance of this finding is uncertain. Further research is needed to determine whether the observed trend of increased Pseudomonas aeruginosa colonization after four to six years of prophylaxis is a random occurrence or a true effect. Additionally, future studies should explore whether the choice of antibiotic or the duration of treatment influences these outcomes.
